summary: This Wikipedia article excerpt covers the formation and evolution of the Solar System, from the collapse of a giant molecular cloud about 4.6 billion years ago through planet accretion, planetary migration, the Late Heavy Bombardment, and the later development of the Oort cloud and Kuiper belt. It also outlines the nebular hypothesis and its history, and the Sun's expected long-term future as a red giant and white dwarf. The excerpt is truncated partway through the Moons section, so later material is not included.
one_line: Wikipedia article summarizing how the Solar System formed from a collapsing molecular cloud and evolved through planetary migration and bombardment, with its expected future.
key_facts: The formation of the Solar System began about 4.6 billion years ago with the gravitational collapse of a small part of a giant molecular cloud.
The nebular hypothesis was first developed in the 18th century by Emanuel Swedenborg, Immanuel Kant, and Pierre-Simon Laplace.
The oldest inclusions found in meteorites are 4,568.2 million years old, which is one definition of the age of the Solar System.
The presolar nebula was about 98% hydrogen, helium and trace lithium produced by Big Bang nucleosynthesis, with heavier elements making up the remaining 2% of its mass.
Studies of the Kuiper belt suggest the Sun formed within a cluster of between 1,000 and 10,000 stars with a collective mass of 3,000 M☉.
Within 50 million years, the temperature and pressure at the core of the Sun became great enough for its hydrogen to begin fusing, marking its entry into the main sequence.
In roughly 5 billion years the Sun will cool and expand into a red giant before casting off its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf.
The planets are thought to have formed by accretion, in which dust grains clumped into planetesimals of about 10 km in size that grew through further collisions.
The frost line is the point between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter where material is cool enough for volatile icy compounds to remain solid.
Jupiter finally topped out at 318 Earth masses after its envelope grew rapidly once it was about equal to its solid core mass.
According to the Nice model, after 500–600 million years Jupiter and Saturn fell into a 2:1 orbital resonance.
The Kuiper belt lies between 30 and 55 AU from the Sun, while the distant Oort cloud begins at about 50,000 AU.
Meteor Crater in Arizona was created about 50,000 years ago by an impactor about 50 metres across.
Earth's current water content is about 6×10^21 kg, which is thought to have been delivered from outer, colder parts of the Solar System.
The Grand tack hypothesis, published June 6, 2011 by Southwest Research Institute in San Antonio, Texas, proposes that Jupiter migrated inward to 1.5 AU.
